Is Online Therapy Right for Your Teen This Summer?

Summer can bring much-needed downtime for teens after months of balancing school, homework, and social pressure. But without that day-to-day structure, it can also raise a few unexpected mental health challenges. Some teenagers enjoy the break, but others find the lack of routine and social connection unsettling. Between late nights, sleep-ins, and more screen time, emotional balance can slip without anyone realising.

That’s why some families consider telehealth counseling during the summer break. It’s a flexible way to support teenagers emotionally when regular schedules are off. For teens who find it hard to open up or who are feeling flat or overwhelmed, an online appointment can be a good first step in feeling more like themselves again.

Why Summer Can Be Hard for Teenagers

Even though school holidays are supposed to be relaxing, plenty of teens feel off during the break, and many don’t say much about it. With school out, the structure that usually shapes each day disappears. No morning bells, no packed lunches, no class schedules. That might sound like freedom, but it can mess with sleep, mood, and motivation.

• Teens often stay up later and sleep in, which can disrupt body rhythms and leave them feeling sluggish or irritable • More time at home can mean more hours staring at phones or computers, which may affect mood and focus • Without regular peer contact, some teens feel left out or unsure where they stand socially • Holidays or travel can put new pressures on family dynamics, especially when teens are feeling sensitive or disconnected

With all these shifts, it’s no surprise that some teens struggle to feel settled during summer.

Signs Your Teen May Need Extra Support

It’s not always clear when your teen is finding things tough. Some kids get quieter. Others seem more angry or quick to snap. You might not see full-on meltdowns, but little changes can point to something deeper going on.

• They seem on edge, pull away from family, or stop doing things they usually enjoy • They talk more about feeling down, anxious, or like things are too hard • They avoid conversations or shut down when others try to check in • They look tired or drained even after restful days

Some of these behaviours can be part of teenage life, but if they hang around or get stronger over time, it may be a cue to look into extra support, even briefly. A neutral space to share thoughts without judgment can make a real difference.

How Telehealth Sessions Work With Teens

Booking in for support can feel like a big leap for some teens, especially if they don’t like new environments or are still warming up to the idea of counselling. Telehealth can offer a softer place to begin.

• Appointments can be scheduled around holidays, work shifts, or family trips, helping things feel more relaxed • Sessions happen in familiar spaces, like their room or a cosy part of the house, where they’re more likely to feel safe • Talking on a screen can feel less intense than sitting face-to-face, which often helps teens who are anxious about opening up • Teens who already use video calls with friends may feel more at ease starting support this way

Sometimes just knowing there’s no pressure to sit in an unfamiliar office makes it easier for teens to show up and speak more freely.

Benefits of Choosing Telehealth Over the Summer Break

When the usual routines dissolve over summer, having something regular, like a check-in, can bring a steadying effect. Telehealth fits that need without becoming a chore.

• It keeps support going in a simple way, even when everyday structures are on pause • There’s no travel needed, so it doesn’t interrupt school holiday plans or take up too much of their day • If local options are fully booked during the break, telehealth saves the wait by making appointments more available • Eligible families may use Medicare rebates for telehealth sessions, making care more accessible over the summer holidays

A small amount of consistent support can help teens move through rough patches without letting feelings build up too much.

Is It the Right Fit for Your Teen?

Not every teen will take to telehealth right away, but some warm up faster than expected. A few things to think about before trying it:

• Do they have a quiet place where they can speak privately? • Are they okay using video or phone calls, or do they find screen time exhausting outside of social apps? • Have they mentioned wanting help, or are they open to one low-pressure session to start with?

Even one or two appointments might help a teen feel seen and settle into the summer with more clarity and calm.

Dedicated Clinical Experience for Brisbane Teens

Michelle Barratt Psychology provides evidence-based telehealth counselling delivered by experienced clinical psychologists registered with the Psychology Board of Australia. Telehealth sessions are available for clients across Brisbane and are designed to be accessible for teens who need support during changes in routine or while on holiday. Our team includes psychologists trained to work with teenagers, tailoring sessions to each individual’s comfort and needs.

Helping Your Teen Feel Better, One Step at a Time

While school holidays are meant to be a break, some teens feel a bit lost in all the free time. They may not always say it out loud, but the signs are there when you know what to look for. With the right support at the right time, that unsettled feeling doesn’t have to take over the summer.

Telehealth sessions can give teens a chance to pause, check in, and talk things through at their own pace. No big leaps, no pressure to fix everything, just space to feel heard and supported when life gets a bit heavy. That space can help the whole family breathe a little easier.

If your teen is facing an emotional uphill over the summer, a little professional guidance can make all the difference. At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our telehealth counselling option offers a convenient solution to support your teenager through these changing times, providing access to care without interrupting their summer plans.
